Reply: Thanks so much for the reviewer’s suggestion. The 70% reduction in ERG amplitude observed in the SI group correlated with commensurate thinning of the outer nuclear layer (ONL) in H&E-stained sections and intense TUNEL labeling in photoreceptor segments. Z(CAT&SOD) treatment not only restored a-wave amplitude but also preserved ONL thickness and reduced photoreceptor apoptosis, indicating primary neuroprotection at the photoreceptor level. While the b-wave originates from bipolar cells, its recovery temporally mirrored both a-wave restoration and ONL survival. This temporal correspondence supports the established dependence of bipolar cell function on intact photoreceptor input: by mitigating ROS-mediated photoreceptor degeneration, Z(CAT&SOD) preserved synaptic transmission to second-order neurons, thereby facilitating b-wave recovery. Thus, these ERG improvements reflect a primary photoreceptor rescue mechanism with consequent restoration of downstream signaling pathways. The related discussion has been added in the revised manuscript as following:
“The restoration of ERG amplitudes in Z(CAT&SOD)-treated mice, alongside intact ONL and RPE morphology, provides direct evidence that photoreceptor-targeted ROS neutralization is both a mechanistic requirement and a novel therapeutic strategy for preserving retinal function.”

The related results and discussion have been added in the revised manuscript as following.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript contains significant conceptual, methodological, and technical flaws related to ocular biology, which limit the validity of the study. The authors have addressed some prior concerns and added new experiments, but key issues remain.
1. Safety of Nanocages
1. Polymerized materials are generally inert, but incomplete polymerization or residual monomers may pose risks and should be acknowledged.
2. Conceptual Accuracy and Ocular Terminology
2. FFA detects vascular abnormalities; in SI-treated mice, increased FFA reflects RPE barrier disruption, not neovascularization.
3. Neovascularization is not expected in the SI injury model.
4. Fig. S12 references CNV incorrectly; SI injury does not induce CNV, and GA does not involve CNV.
5. ERG a- and b-waves measure retinal function, not visual acuity.
6. Missing statistical summaries of ERG amplitudes is a critical issue; plotting style conventions are minor (see Section 5).
3. SI-Induced Retinal Damage Model
Model Understanding and Terminology
7. The rationale for using 10 mg/kg SI is not provided.
8. The SI model should not be referred to as GA; it is an acute chemical injury distinct from human geographic atrophy.
9. Mice lack a macula; human GA scoring is not applicable. GA-like lesions in mice should be described as RPE/photoreceptor atrophy.
Figure 1 and Related Panels
10. “Neurodeatrophia” is nonstandard; “neurodegeneration” or “neuronal atrophy” is correct.
11. “Atrophy of optic nerve cells” is incorrect; the shapes shown do not resemble photoreceptor outer segments.
12. “Drusen” is misapplied; SI models do not produce true drusen and may represent pseudodrusen.
13. Antioxidant dysfunction is not illustrated in the RPE.
14. Panels showing “conjunctival barrier” and “sclerotic barrier” inside cells are anatomically incorrect.
15. The scheme does not accurately show how CAT and SOD reach the RPE; Z(CAT&SOD) contains both enzymes but this is not clear.
16. HCECs and HConEpiCs are irrelevant; SI injury affects RPE and photoreceptors.
Methods and Experimental Design
17. Methods list ARPE-32, HUVECs, and RAW 264.7 cells, but none appear in the results. HCECs are not listed in Methods and are corneal endothelial cells, not relevant to the study.
18. The subtitle “Construction of a GA model” is misleading; the model is an acute chemical injury.
19. Methods for ocular assays (fundoscopy, OCT, ERG), instrumentation, and analyses are not described, indicating lack of ocular biology expertise.
20. Intravitreal injections of 5 µL are physiologically impossible in mice (vitreous ≈2 µL).
Fundus and FAF
21. Hyperfluorescent spots from FAF images are not quantified.
4. Overinterpretation and Therapeutic Claims
22. Claims of “pioneering a new therapeutic paradigm for dry AMD” overstate the study.
23. The SI model is not representative of human GA or AMD.
24. Simply increasing SOD/CAT is not universally protective; overexpression can have unintended effects.
25. Evidence regarding GPx/TAS in AMD, delivery of CAT/SOD to RPE mitochondria, and SOD mimetics or gene therapy as clinically feasible strategies is not addressed.
5. Minor Issues
26. Fig. R1 (now Fig. S14) legend does not specify whether assays were performed in untreated or SI-treated animals.
27. Figures S9b and S13b lack clear legends, treatment descriptions, and baseline (“before treatment”) images.
28. Terms such as “thickness length of CNV” are unclear.
29. Missing “respectively” when defining a- and b-waves (p.4, line 144; p.5, line 180).
30. Plotting style of some ERG panels (e.g., Fig. 4g) is unconventional.
31. “Eye drop” should be two words.
32. Abstract and introduction are excessively long; discussion does not include limitations.
33. Missing references (p.3, lines 94–96; p.11, lines 452–455).
34. Many figure legends lack treatment details, orientation, and arrow explanations.
35. IR fundus images (Fig. 4b, 6e) do not indicate whether they are from the same animals.
36. OCT images lack optic nerve localization and measurement indicators.
37. Source tissue for mRNA analyses is unspecified.
38. TUNEL staining in the RPE is not indicated.
39. Individual data points are missing from plots, especially Fig. 3l and ERG amplitude analyses.
40. Some ERG plots are partially obscured by axis labels.
41. Fig. 5a: retinal orientation unclear; TUNEL higher in “Healthy” vs. “Untreated” is unexplained.
42. Fig. 5l schematic is not informative.
43. Fig. 6e: timing of lutein treatment relative to SI is unclear; prophylactic vs. post-injury effects differ.
44. Fig. 6f: statistical analysis of a- and b-wave amplitudes for all animals is missing.
45. CAT-FITC enzymatic activity is not reported.
Summary: The manuscript contains fundamental flaws in experimental design, methodology, and biological interpretation. Major issues include misrepresentation of the SI injury model as GA, inappropriate in vitro cell models, physiologically impossible intravitreal injections, missing descriptions of ocular assays and analyses, and multiple inaccuracies in figures and data interpretation. These flaws significantly compromise the validity of the study.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: The authors have satisfactorily addressed my concerns; I recommend acceptance.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: The authors did a nice job to address my concerns and I would like to reccomend accept this manuscript without scientific change.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Responses to reviewer’s comments
We sincerely thank all the reviewers for their time and valuable comments. We are particularly pleased to see the recognition of our work from reviewer 2# and 3#. However, we are very concerned about some of the comments from reviewer 1#. We believe that some of these comments are based on misunderstandings of the work. And we will provide detailed responses point by point below in an attempt to clarify the misunderstandings.
Reviewer #1:
The manuscript contains significant conceptual, methodological, and technical flaws related to ocular biology, which limit the validity of the study. The authors have addressed some prior concerns and added new experiments, but key issues remain.
1. Polymerized materials are generally inert, but incomplete polymerization or residual monomers may pose risks and should be acknowledged.
Reply: Thanks so much for the reviewer’s suggestion. The synthesis protocol for zwitterionic polymer is well-established and widely recognized for producing biomedical-grade polymers, as reported in previous literatures1-5. Furthermore, our comprehensive in vivo safety data, presented in the initial response (Figure R1 / S14), provide the most biologically relevant confirmation. Critically, no local or systemic toxicity was observed, even after long-term topical administration. Therefore, these findings demonstrate the safety of our nanocage system for its intended ophthalmic application.
Reference
1. Fang, H. et al. In Situ Polymerization of Zwitterions on Therapeutic Proteins to Enable Their Effective Oral Delivery. ACS Nano 17, 1128-1143 (2023).
2. Fan, W. et al. Mucus Penetrating and Cell-Binding Polyzwitterionic Micelles as Potent Oral Nanomedicine for Cancer Drug Delivery. Advanced Materials 34, 2109189 (2022).
3. Zhou, Y. et al. A pH-Triggered Self-Unpacking Capsule Containing Zwitterionic Hydrogel-Coated MOF Nanoparticles for Efficient Oral Exendin-4 Delivery. Advanced Materials 33, 2102044 (2021).
4. Zhou, Q. et al. Enzyme-activatable polymer-drug conjugate augments tumour penetration and treatment efficacy. Nature Nanotechnology 14, 799-809 (2019).
5. Han, X. et al. Zwitterionic micelles efficiently deliver oral insulin without opening tight junctions. Nature Nanotechnology 15, 605-614 (2020).
Figure R1. Safety assessment of Z-polymer and Z(CAT&SOD) in normal mice (n=3). (a) Representative images of cornea’s light fields and (b) fluorescein cornea staining of mouse eyes after different treatments for 2 and 4 weeks by slit-lamp microscopy. (c) The tear secretion amount of mouse eyes after different treatments for 2 and 4 weeks (d) Representative images of OCT images of cornea and (e) retina for 2 and 4 weeks. (f) Statistical analysis of relative retina thickness. (g) Representative images of retina’s light fields and (h) fluorescein staining of retina after different treatments for 2 and 4 weeks. (i) Statistical analysis of IOPs of eyes in mice after different treatments for 2 and 4 weeks. (j) H&E staining images of different organs including liver, spleen, lung, kidney, heart and eye collected from mice in different groups (scale bars: 500 μm). (k) Blood biochemistry and complete blood analysis of mice with different treatments. The following parameters were tested: percentage of white blood cell (WBC); percentage of lymphocytes (Lymph); percentage of monocytes (MON); percentage of neutrophilic granulocyte (Gran); red blood cell (RBC) counts; hemoglobin (HGB); hematocrit (HCT); mean corpuscular volume (MCV); mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH); platelets (PLT); alanine aminotransferase (ALT); aspartate aminotransferase (AST); alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and blood urea nitrogen (BUN). Data were represented as means ± SD.
2. FFA detects vascular abnormalities; in SI-treated mice, increased FFA reflects RPE barrier disruption, not neovascularization.
Reply: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment, which allows us to better clarify a critical aspect of our experimental model. We fully agree that in typical human geographic atrophy (GA), increased FFA signal is primarily attributed to RPE barrier disruption rather than neovascularization. However, it’s important to note that the sodium iodate (SI)-induced model in our study, while effectively mimicking oxidative stress-driven photoreceptor/RPE degeneration characteristic GA, often elicits a more extensive secondary inflammatory response involving retinal vasculature. The vascular abnormalities we observed via FFA (has been changed as “vascular inflammation” or “secondary vascular abnormalities” in the revised main text) do not represent neovascularization, but rather reflect inflammation-associated vascular leakage specific in this model. The observed fluorescence enhancement indeed stems from blood-retinal barrier disruption, encompassing both RPE and endothelial cell damage under inflammatory conditions. Here, FFA serves as a valuable in vivo method to evaluate the extent of secondary vascular inflammation and overall blood-retinal barrier integrity, both important indicators of retinal health in our model. We have moved this data to Supporting Information to avoid overstating its role in the core narrative of GA-like atrophy, while still presenting it as a supporting metric of disease severity and treatment efficacy against the multifaceted insult induced by SI.
We have carefully revised the manuscript to clarify that the FFA findings reflect model-specific inflammatory responses rather than neovascularization. This distinction is now explicitly addressed in the discussion to avoid any potential misunderstanding regarding neovascular and atrophic pathways.
“FFA images showing therapeutic effects on secondary vascular inflammation in SI-induced retinal degeneration”
“As shown in Figure 2k and 2l, prominent retinal deposits were observed in both PBS- and SOD-injected groups, accompanied by subretinal debris accumulation (likely originating from degenerated RPE and photoreceptors), inflammatory edema, and oxidative stress-induced vascular abnormalities (Figure S2a).”
3. Neovascularization is not expected in the SI injury model.
Reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment regarding the sodium iodate (SI) model’s pathophysiology. While SI primarily targets the RPE and photoreceptors, and is not a classic model for choroidal neovascularization (CNV), extensive literatures demonstrates that its severe oxidative injury triggers robust secondary inflammatory response. This inflammation response extends beyond the RPE/photoreceptor layer, affecting retinal vasculature and leading to blood-retinal barrier (BRB) breakdown, vascular leakage, and in some reports, even aberrant vascular changes6-9. Importantly, these effects are inflammation-mediated and distinct from VEGF-driven neovascularization in wet AMD. In our revised manuscript, we have consistently termed these observation as “secondary vascular abnormalities”, “vascular inflammation” or “vascular leakage” to accurately reflect this inflammatory vasculopathy.
“In contrast, the Z(CAT&SOD) group displayed a more intact retinal structure and lower inflammation levels, comparable to the healthy retinal microenvironment. This dual-enzyme approach not only mitigates inflammation but also helps maintain the integrity of the retinal structure by reducing vascular permeability and preventing secondary vascular abnormalities.”
Reference
6. Hollyfield, J. G. et al. Oxidative damage-induced inflammation initiates age-related macular degeneration. Nat. Med. 14, 194-198 (2008).
7. Yao, T. et al. Comparative mechanistic study of RPE cell death induced by different oxidative stresses. Redox Biol. 65, 102840 (2023).
8. Kerur, N. et al. cGAS drives noncanonical-inflammasome activation in age-related macular degeneration. Nat. Med. 24, 50-61 (2018).
9. Zhang, R. et al. A pH/ROS dual-responsive and targeting nanotherapy for vascular inflammatory diseases. Biomaterials 230, 119605 (2020).
4. Fig. S12 references CNV incorrectly; SI injury does not induce CNV, and GA does not involve CNV.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for this valuable feedback. Upon careful consideration, we recognized that the original phrase “lesions in GA mice” could be misleading, as classic GA is pathologically characterized by atrophic lesions (RPE/photoreceptor loss) rather than vascular lesions detectable by FFA. To ensure conceptual clarity, we have revised the figure legend to describe these observations more accurately in the revised manuscript as following. In addition, we would like to clarify the scientific rationale for including this assay. While the SI model primarily recapitulates the oxidative stress and photoreceptor/RPE degeneration characteristic of GA, it also elicits a significant secondary inflammatory response. Importantly, this inflammation can disrupt the blood-retinal barrier (BRB), resulting in quantifiable vascular abnormalities detectable by FFA.
“FFA images showing therapeutic effects on secondary vascular inflammation in SI-induced retinal degeneration”
“As shown in Figure 2k and 2l, prominent retinal deposits were observed in both PBS- and SOD-injected groups, accompanied by subretinal debris accumulation (likely originating from degenerated RPE and photoreceptors), inflammatory edema, and oxidative stress-induced vascular abnormalities (Figure S2a).”
5. ERG a- and b-waves measure retinal function, not visual acuity.
Reply: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment and fully agree with this important clarification. We acknowledge that certain terms in our original description required greater precision. Specifically, we have revised phrases such as “restoration of visual acuity” in the context of ERG data with more precise descriptions as following in the revised manuscript.
“Analysis of the a- and b- waves, which reflect photoreceptor and ON-bipolar cell activity, respectively, demonstrated partial recovery of electrophysiological responses in mice treated with either CAT or SOD&CAT injections.”
6. Missing statistical summaries of ERG amplitudes is a critical issue; plotting style conventions are minor (see Section 5).
Reply: Thanks so much for pointing it out. We would like to clarify that the complete statistical analyses for the ERG amplitude data are provided in the Supporting Information as Figure S12 in our original manuscript.
Figure R2. Representative ERG wave responses of acute retinal injury mice under scotopic conditions following different treatments, along with statistical analysis of A and B waves measured by ERG (n=4).
7. The rationale for using 10 mg/kg SI is not provided.
Reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s question regarding the SI dosage. The 10 mg/kg sodium iodate (administered intravenously) was selected based on well-established protocols to ensure a robust and reproducible model of oxidative retinal injury10-12. The related discussion has been added in the revised manuscript as following:
“This dosage is well-established to consistently induce oxidative damage in RPE cells and photoreceptors, creating an acute retinal injury mouse model that recapitulates key oxidative stress-related cellular events in GA33-35.”
Reference
10. Liu, B. et al. Sodium iodate induces ferroptosis in human retinal pigment epithelium ARPE-19 cells. Cell Death & Disease 12, 230 (2021).
11. Chen, Y. et al. Oxidative stress induces mitochondrial iron overload and ferroptotic cell death. Scientific Reports 13, 15515 (2023).
12. Zhou, Y. et al. Oxidative stress-mediated mitochondrial fission promotes hepatic stellate cell activation via stimulating oxidative phosphorylation. Cell Death & Disease 13, 689 (2022).
8. The SI model should not be referred to as GA; it is an acute chemical injury distinct from human geographic atrophy.
Reply: Thanks so much for the reviewer’s important comment regarding disease modeling terminology. We fully agree that the sodium iodate (SI) model represents an acute chemical injury model and does not fully replicate the chronic, multifactorial pathogenesis of human geographic atrophy (GA). We selected the SI model because it is a well-established and widely used preclinical model that reliably induces oxidative stress-mediated RPE and photoreceptor degeneration, the key cellular events in GA pathogenesis13-14. This model allows us to specifically test whether our antioxidant nanocage platform can protect these critical cell types from the oxidative damage, a central mechanism in GA progression. We have revised the text to clarify the model’s limitations while maintaining its scientific rational: to evaluate whether targeted antioxidant delivery can rescue retinal cells from oxidative stress, a therapeutic strategy directly relevant to dry AMD/GA. We thank the reviewer for this valuable opportunity to improve our manuscript’s clarity.
Title: “Permeable nanoreactor eyedrop for enzymatic cascade-mediated treatment for acute retinal injury model mimicking geographic atrophy”
“Collectively, our work demonstrates that the zwitterionic nanocage platform enables effective topical delivery of antioxidant enzymes to the retina, presenting a promising therapeutic strategy for combating oxidative stress in conditions such as dry AMD.”
Reference
13. Fleckenstein, M. et al. Age-Related Macular Degeneration: A Review. JAMA 331, 147-157 (2024).
14. Ambati, J. et al. An animal model of age-related macular degeneration in senescent Ccl-2- or Ccr- 2-deficient mice. Nature Medicine 9, 1390-1397 (2003).
9. Mice lack a macula; human GA scoring is not applicable. GA-like lesions in mice should be described as RPE/photoreceptor atrophy.
Reply: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment regarding species-specific anatomical considerations. As correctly noted, mice lack a macula, which precludes direct application of human GA clinical scoring criteria that rely on macular lesion characteristics. In response to this important observation, we would like to clarify that the scoring system presented in Table R1 represents a customized, semi-quantitative histopathological grading scale specifically developed for this study. This tailored approach enables systematic assessment of two key pathological features in our mouse model: the severity of RPE layer degeneration and the degree of overall retinal thinning. By establishing this species-appropriate evaluation method, we aimed to maintain rigorous pathological assessment while respecting fundamental anatomical differences between murine and human ocular structures.
“After different treatments, a blinded evaluation was performed based on fundus imaging and OCT imaging to assess retinal structural integrity and thickness reduction(Figure S2b).”
Table R1. The scoring rubric of acute retinal injury mice model
10. “Neurodeatrophia” is nonstandard; “neurodegeneration” or “neuronal atrophy” is correct.
Reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s careful attention to terminology. As correctly noted, “Neurodeatrophia” is a nonstandard term. We have replaced all instances with the standard term, “neurodegeneration” throughout the manuscript and figure in this revised manuscript (Figure R3).
Figure R3. Schematic illustration of antioxidant mechanism disruption and therapeutic intervention in acute retinal injury mice model. (a) In the progression of acute retinal injury model, neurodegeneration is associated with the accumulation of oxidative stress and reduction in peroxidase levels. This imbalance triggers retinal inflammatory pathways, leading to the atrophy and antioxidant dysfunction of RPEs. (b) A groundbreaking and noninvasive eye drop formulation utilizing zwitterionic polymer-modified peroxidase (Z(CAT&SOD)) was developed for GA treatment. The Z(CAT&SOD) eye drops could effectively penetrate the ocular barriers through both conjunctiva-sclera-retina and conjunctiva-blood-retina pathways to reduce oxidative stress and mitigate inflammation by harnessing the via enzymatic cascade, offering a promising therapeutic approach for GA management.
11. “Atrophy of optic nerve cells” is incorrect; the shapes shown do not resemble photoreceptor outer segments.
Reply: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s valuable feedback on our schematic diagram. In response to above comment, we have revised “Atrophy of optic nerve cells” to the accurate term “neurodegeneration”. The diagram was designed to conceptually illustrate the pathological progression from an organized, healthy structure to a damaged, degenerative state. The abstract shapes were intended to represent dystrophic and fragmented photoreceptor remnants within the atrophic zone, consistent with our histological observations.
12. “Drusen” is misapplied; SI models do not produce true drusen and may represent pseudodrusen.
Reply: Thanks so much for the reviewer’s suggestion. Our schematic aimed to conceptually represent subretinal deposit accumulation in our model’s retinal degenerative phenotype, which shares a conceptual similarity with the deposit-driven pathology in human AMD. While we acknowledge that “Drusen” specifically refers to extracellular deposits located between the RPE and Bruch’s membrane in human eyes, a feature not fully recapitulated in our model, we have revised the terminology to “Drusen-like deposits” in both the schematic and manuscript to reflect these distinctions more accurately while maintaining the conceptual parallel.
Figure R4. Schematic illustration of the retina of acute retinal injury mice model.
13. Antioxidant dysfunction is not illustrated in the RPE.
Reply: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s constructive suggestion to enhance the conceptual clarity of our schematic. We fully agree that explicitly illustrating antioxidant dysfunction within the RPE cell would better represent this critical pathological mechanism. Accordingly, we have modified the schematic to incorporate this important element, which will significantly enhance its scientific accuracy and educational value.
14. Panels showing “conjunctival barrier” and “sclerotic barrier” inside cells are anatomically incorrect.
Reply: Thanks so much for the reviewer’s suggestion. Our schematic aimed to illustrate the key ocular barriers that a topically applied formulation must overcome. In response to the comment, we have adjusted the illustration to better highlight the cell-cell interfaces and junctional complexes that form these functional barriers. Additionally, we will update the figure legend to explicitly state: “Schematic representation of the cellular barriers formed by conjunctival and scleral cells.”
15. The scheme does not accurately show how CAT and SOD reach the RPE; Z(CAT&SOD) contains both enzymes but this is not clear.
Reply: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s comment regarding the schematic. We would like to clarify that this illustration is intended as a simplified, conceptual overview highlighting the key steps of our therapeutic strategy. The detailed mechanism of cellular uptake and intracellular delivery of the enzymes (CAT and SOD) by our zwitterionic nanocage, Z(CAT&SOD), is rigorously supported by experimental evidence presented in the manuscript. In the part where we studied the penetration section of Z(CAT&SOD), we provided a detailed description of its penetration mechanism again. See Figure R5 (Figure 3m). What’s more, we also demonstrate the co-loading and quantitative encapsulation efficiency of both CAT and SOD in Table S1. What’s more, we also tested the enzyme activity of CAT and SOD in the zwitterionic polymer nanocages.
Figure R5. Schematic illustration of penetration mechanism of zwitterion peroxidase.
16. HCECs and HConEpiCs are irrelevant; SI injury affects RPE and photoreceptors.
Reply: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s comment. This provides us with a valuable opportunity to clarify the dual purpose of our schematic. This illustration is not limited to depicting the SI injury model; rather, it presents a comprehensive overview of our drug delivery strategy: from topical application and traversal of anterior segment barriers to therapeutic action at the retinal disease site. Importantly, removing the anterior segment cells (HCECs, HConEpiCs) would mispresent our study, as these elements are essential for demonstrating the delivery challenge that our zwitterionic nanocage specifically addresses.
17. Methods list ARPE-32, HUVECs, and RAW 264.7 cells, but none appear in the results. HCECs are not listed in Methods and are corneal endothelial cells, not relevant to the study.
Reply: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s careful evaluation of our Methods and Results sections. We acknowledge and apologize for the identified discrepancies, which resulted from an oversight during manuscript preparation. We are grateful for the opportunity to address these issues and have conducted a comprehensive, cross-referential review of the entire manuscript to ensure full consistency between the methodologies described and the results presented.
“Human conjunctival epithelial cells (HConEpiC) were obtained from American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, Manassas, VA, USA), and cultured in DMEM containing 1% penicillin/streptomycin and 10% FBS at 37 °C in 5% CO . Seven-week-old female C57BL/6 mice 2 were purchased from Nanjing Pengsheng Biological Technology Co. The animals were acclimated in SPF environment for one week prior to conducting follow-up experiments. All animal procedures complied with relevant laws and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Soochow University (No. ECSU-2019000198).”
18. The subtitle “Construction of a GA model” is misleading; the model is an acute chemical injury.
Reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable suggestion and fully agree with the recommendation. Accordingly, we have modified the subtitle from “Construction of a GA model” to the more accurate description “Construction and evaluation of acute retinal injury mice model” in this revised manuscript as following:
“Construction and evaluation of acute retinal injury mice model”
19. Methods for ocular assays (fundoscopy, OCT, ERG), instrumentation, and analyses are not described, indicating lack of ocular biology expertise.
Reply: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s comment regarding the methodological aspect. We apologize for this oversight, which stemmed from our assumption that these protocols were standard practice rather than from any technical limitations. We have provided the detailed methodological specifications that were inadvertently omitted in this revised manuscript as following:
“In Vivo Imaging (Fundoscopy, OCT and ERG): All imaging was performed using a Micron IV retinal imaging system (Phoenix Research Labs) coupled with a high-resolution OCT module and ERG module. Prior to imaging, mice were anesthetized via intraperitoneal injection of ketamine (80 mg/kg) and xylazine, followed by pupil dilation with with topical administration of 1% tropicamide.
Fundoscopy: Color fundus images were captured using the integrated color fundus camera under standard white light illumination.
Spectral-Domain OCT (SD-OCT): Retinal cross-sectional scans were acquired using the scanning protocol centered on the optic nerve head. Subsequent quantification of retinal layer thicknesses was performed using image J system.
Electroretinography (ERG): Full-field ERG recording was performed in accordance with the International Society for Clinical Electrophysiology of Vision (ISCEV) standard protocol for rodents. Following overnight dark adaptation (>12 hours), mice were anesthetized as above and their pupils were dilated under dim red illumination. Scotopic (rod-dominated) responses were first recorded using a series of flashes with increasing intensities (3 log cd·s/m2). For photopic (cone-mediated) responses, mice were light-adapted for 10 minutes under a 30 cd/m2 background before recording responses to a 1.0 log cd·s/m2 flash stimulus. ERG waveform analysis included: a-wave amplitude (baseline to trough of initial negative deflection), b-wave amplitude (a-wave trough to the peak of subsequent positive wave), implicit times for both components. All recordings and analyses were performed using the integrated ERG module of the Micron IV retinal imaging system.”

Reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. We fully acknowledge that nearly no animal model perfectly recapitulates the complex, chronic progression of human GA/AMD. However, our study is primarily a mechanism-driven proof-of-concept investigation, designed to test whether non-invasive delivery of antioxidant enzyme can protect the retina from oxidative injury-a key pathogenic driver in dry AMD. For this specific purpose, the SI model serves as is a validated experimental system that reliably induces oxidative stress-mediated RPE and photoreceptor degeneration, which are hallmark cellular events in GA. Given the current lack of effective GA therapies, exploring novel strategies in reproducible models remains critically important. 24. Simply increasing SOD/CAT is not universally protective; overexpression can have unintended effects.
Reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment regarding the potential risks of antioxidant enzyme overexpression. We completely agree that constitutive overexpression can disrupt redox homeostasis, a well-known challenge in antioxidant therapy. However, our approach differs fundamentally: rather than genetically inducing chronic enzyme production, we employ localized delivery of precisely dosed SOD and CAT co-encapsulated in a protective nanocage. This pharmacologic strategy ensures stoichiometric enzyme delivery to injury sites without genetic alteration. Importantly, our in vivo safety data (Figure R1/S14) demonstrate no detectable toxicity, after single or repeated administration, directly addressing the reviewer’s concern. While we acknowledge the biological complexities of antioxidant interventions, our study provides the first evidence that transient, dual-enzyme delivery can achieve efficacy without the off-target effects associated with traditional antioxidant strategies. In summary, while we share the reviewer’s caution, our data show that controlled, localized enzyme delivery circumvents the historical pitfalls of nonspecific antioxidant approaches.
“In summary, this work demonstrated that the pathogenesis of acute retinal injury involves excessive retinal ROS production and dimished peroxidase activity. Replenishment of CAT and SOD effectively attenuated retinal oxidative stress and inflammation, thereby reducing cellular apoptosis. Moreover, we developed a localized delivery system featuring precisely dosed SOD and CAT co-encapsulated in a protective nanocage, enabling stoichiometric enzyme delivery to injury sites while avoiding genetic alteration.”
25. Evidence regarding GPx/TAS in AMD, delivery of CAT/SOD to RPE mitochondria, and SOD mimetics or gene therapy as clinically feasible strategies is not addressed.

This formed the basis for our targeted therapeutic strategy of replenishing these compromised endogenous enzymes. We have incorporated discussion of GPx/TAS and their complementary antioxidant roles in the revised manuscript.
Regarding subcellular targeting, we agree that mitochondrial delivery would be ideal given its role as a major ROS source. While organelle-specific targeting remains challenge for protein therapies, our work establishes a crucial foundation by achieving efficient delivery of active enzymes to retinal cells (RPE/photoreceptors), as demonstrated by the confocal imaging (Figure 3f) and functional rescue data (Figs. 4-6). Future platform iterations incorporating mitochondrial-targeting motifs represent an exciting direction, which have highlighted in the revised manuscript.
Collectively, our system represents a non-genetic protein replacement strategy that leverages the natural catalytic efficiency of evolutionarily optimized enzymes. Our nanocage system effectively preserves their full native activity while enabling non-invasive delivery.
“Our findings highlight the therapeutic potential of enzymatic antioxidant therapy while revealing important avenues for further research. First, comprehensive investigation of endogenous antioxidant systems, particularly the glutathione peroxidase (GPx)/total antioxidant status (TAS) and related peroxidases, could uncover synergistic mechanisms. Developing organelle-specific delivery platforms may further optimize therapeutic efficacy in oxidative retinal injury models. Second, while the SI-induced acute model has provided valuable mechanistic insights, its limitations in modeling the chronic, multifactorial nature of human dry AMD should be acknowledged. Complementary model systems that better recapitulate disease progression will be crucial for translating these antioxidant strategies into clinically viable therapies.”

Reply: Thanks so much for pointing it out. We have revised abstract and introduction.
“Abstract:
Age-related macular degeneration (AMD), particularly in its most prevalent form geographic atrophy (GA), has historically been challenging to treat due to its complex pathogenesis. A key driver of GA progression is the oxidative stress-induced apoptosis of retinal cells, ultimately leading to blindness. In our study using a retinal acute injury mouse model to mimic the reactive oxygen species (ROS)-induced retinal degeneration pathogenesis of GA, we consistently observed effective recovery of enzymatic cascade may be an effective therapeutic strategy for this model. To overcome ocular delivery barriers, we engineered zwitterionic nanocages for co-delivering CAT and SOD. This system significantly alleviated oxidative damage and inflammation in an SI-induced retinal injury model. Given the chronic and progressive nature of GA, zwitterionic-peroxidase was optimized to develop a non-invasive eye drop formulation for GA management. Surprisingly, the zwitterionic-peroxidase achieved a remarkable 9.32% penetration rate into the eyeball, significantly outperforming the free peroxidase (0.54%), through conjunctival-sclera-retina and conjunctival-blood-retina penetration pathways, and achieved therapeutic efficacy comparable to intravitreal injections. Additionally, extra supplementation of Z(CAT&SOD) in acute retinal injury model showed superior therapeutic effects compared to the current gold standard clinical treatment of supplementing antioxidants and lutein. Our pioneering study revealed the possible association between retinal peroxidase deficiency and GA progression, and proposed an innovative zwitterionic nanocage-based peroxidase, which exhibits great potential as a non-invasive yet highly effective therapeutic strategy for AMD.”
“Introduction:
Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a progressive and degenerative disease characterized by dysfunction and death of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells and photoreceptors, leading to irreversible vision loss1, 2. It is the leading cause of permanent visual impairment worldwide, affecting more than 180 million people, mainly over the age of 55. AMD manifests in two primary forms: geographic atrophy (GA) and choroidal neovascularization (CNV). Among them, GA patients constitute approximately 85% to 90%, and the rate of blindness approaches nearly 20%3. Since the introduction of intravitreal injection of anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF), patients with CNV have experienced substantial improvements in retinal function. However, despite the effectiveness of anti-VEGF therapies for CNV, these antibodies have proven ineffective in treating GA4. Therefore, there is currently no approved treatment for GA, primarily due to its complex and poorly understood pathogenesis. Clinically, supplementing antioxidants such as lutein appears to be the only viable approach to slowing down the deterioration of GA5. Numerous studies have revealed that relative pathogenesis of GA involves processes such as complement system activation, disturbances in lipid metabolism, oxidative stress, abnormal autophagy, and the chronic inflammation pathways and etc6-8. In response, various therapeutic strategies have been explored, including the suppression of complement activation, inhibition of angiogenesis, and exertion of anti-inflammatory effects9-11. However, these approaches have not yet demonstrated specific, positive impacts in clinical trials involving GA patients12-14. Therefore, the exploration of alternative therapeutic targets for GA treatment remains crucial.
Oxidative stress disrupts the physiological functions in most biological tissues and can lead to cell death15, 16. In the retina, oxidative stress triggers a cascade of events that result in focal loss of RPE and photoreceptors, leading to structural changes in proteins, lipids and DNA, which is increasingly recognized as a major contributing factor to the development of GA12, 15, 17. Numerous studies have demonstrated that the removal of free radicals from the retina can effectively slow the progression of AMD18. Additionally, in AMD treatment research, strategies targeting the elimination of reactive oxygen species (ROS) have been proposed, including the use of inorganic nanozymes like Pt, RhZ, CeO to perform antioxidant function19-22. However, these nanozymes face challenges such as 2 biocompatibility, biodegradability, and unclear therapeutic efficacy. Endogenous antioxidant enzyme, such as superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase (CAT), neutralize free radicals and maintain cellular homeostasis, with SOD targeting superoxide anion (O •−) and CAT decomposing hydrogen peroxide 2 (H O ). These enzymes play essential roles in defending against oxidant stress, particularly in 2 2 regulating ROS in inflammatory diseases23-26. However, the specific roles of CAT and SOD in the pathogenesis of age-related macular degeneration, especially during the geographic atrophy stage, require further investigation.
In this study, we discovered that the cellular antioxidant defense mechanisms were obviously compromised in SI-induced acute retinal injury model, pathological feature of which mimic that of human GA disease27, as evidenced by a noticeable decrease in the expression of CAT and SOD in the retina. While supplementation with CAT and SOD partially alleviated retinal atrophy and visual impairment, the therapeutic effects were not satisfactory. These limitations arise from poor ocular delivery and enzyme instability. Hence, we explored the use of zwitterions, which can polymerize in situ on protein surfaces to effectively shield charges, enhance permeability and preserve enzyme activity in complex physical environment28-32. By ingeniously employing zwitterionic materials, we coated the CAT and SOD with sulfobetaine methacrylate (SBMA), Z(CAT&SOD), a compound widely recognized for its charge regulation, mucosal and tissue penetration and biocompatibility. Remarkably, the Z(CAT&SOD) exhibited improved stability and activity against protease. Moreover, Z(CAT&SOD) demonstrated the ability to facilitate free diffusion across ocular barriers penetration capabilities by promoting clathrin-dependent and caveolae-mediated endocytosis. As expected, following intravitreal injection of Z(CAT&SOD) in acute retinal injury model, the enzymatic cascade reactions exhibited superior ROS scavenging capacity and suppressed the activation of NF-κB-HMGB1-ILs inflammatory pathway. Ultimately, they protected RPEs and photoreceptors from ROS-induced apoptosis, which is crucial for preserving retinal function and preventing degenerative changes. Given the chronic nature and long-term treatment requirements of this disease, we attempted to develop a non-invasive peroxidase eye drop formulation, compared with the clinical gold-standard treatment strategy, supplementing with lutein. Unexpectedly, optimizing the components of zwitterionic polymers led to a significant enhancement in the ocular barrier permeability of zwitterionic-peroxidase, which achieved an impressive 9.32% ocular penetration (the ocular penetration of free peroxidase was only 0.54%) by increasing the permeability through both conjunctiva-sclera-retinal and blood-retinal pathways. Remarkably, the therapeutic effects of zwitterionic-peroxidase eye drops were comparable to those achieved through intravitreal injections in the acute retinal injury model, and both of them demonstrated greater efficacy compared to oral lutein therapy. Our research results emphasize that the progression of GA is associated with clear oxidative stress damage to the retina. The innovative and non-invasive eye drop we developed, which is based on a bimetallic ion nanocage coating of peroxidase, provides a transformative and promising therapeutic approach for dry AMD (Figure 1).”
“Discussion:
In the SI-induced acute retinal injury model, we observed pathological features resembling those in clinical GA patients, including subretinal drusen-like deposits and neurodegeneration. Mechanistic investigations revealed that RPE and photoreceptor cell apoptosis was closely associated with the microenvironment characterized by high oxidative stress and diminished peroxidase activity, particularly reduced levels of CAT and SOD. As a proof-of-concept, our findings suggest that timely antioxidant supplementation may preserve residual photoreceptors when oxidative damage as the primary driver of degeneration. However, the coulombic interactions within the vitreous body and the ILM barrier in the vitreous cavity posed significant challenges to the diffusion and penetration of peroxidases into the RPE and optic nerve cells, even when employing intravitreal injection as a benchmark ophthalmic drug delivery modality. To overcome these challenges, we developed zwitterionic nanocages for CAT and SOD to enhance diffusion and barrier penetration by shielding surface charges and promoting endocytosis pathways. Following the intravitreal injection of Z(CAT&SOD), we observed a significant mitigation of retinal damage in SI-induced acute retinal injury model. This was evidenced by reduced ROS-induced damage in RPE and optic nerve cells, suppression of the NF-κB-HMGB1-ILs inflammation pathways. Therefore, the strategy of using zwitterionic peroxidase with intravitreal injection shows promise for slowing the progression of dry AMD.
However, early-stage dry AMD patients often delay therapy due to concerns about traumatic scarring and postoperative infection, thereby missing the optimal treatment window. Moreover, patients with advanced atrophic dry AMD require sustained therapeutic drug concentrations over an extended period. Developing an effective, non-invasive ophthalmic treatment strategy based on peroxidase is of great importance. To address this, we optimized the components of zwitterionic polymers to select the nanocages with the strongest barrier penetration as carriers for a peroxidase eye drop formulation. Unexpectedly, eyeball penetration of Z(CAT&SOD) eye drop was 9.32%, much higher than that of free peroxidase (the eyeball penetration was only 0.54%). Furthermore, after applying the Z(CAT&SOD) eye drop for two weeks, we observed a significant reduction in retinal cell apoptosis induced by SI, alongside stabilization of retinal thickness and visual function, achieving comparable therapeutic effects to those observed in the intravitreal injection of Z(CAT&SOD). More interestingly, compared with the therapeutic effects of both intravitreal injection and eye drops of Z(CAT&SOD), lutein exhibited inferior therapeutic efficacy. This may be attributed to the retina was affected by the blood-eye barrier in the systemic circulatory system, resulting in limited absorption and the limitation of ROS-scavenging ability of lutein. In summary, this work reported that the pathogenesis of acute retinal injury model is linked to the overproduction of retinal ROS and reduced peroxidase levels. Replenishing CAT and SOD could reduce retinal oxidative stress and inflammation, decreasing cell apoptosis. And we employed localized delivery of precisely dosed SOD and CAT co-encapsulated in a protective nanocage, which ensured stoichiometric enzyme delivery to injury sites without genetic alteration. Collectively, our work demonstrates that the zwitterionic nanocage platform enables effective topical delivery of antioxidant enzymes to the retina, presenting a promising therapeutic strategy for combating oxidative stress in conditions such as dry AMD.
Our findings highlight the therapeutic potential of enzymatic antioxidant therapy while revealing important avenues for further research. First, comprehensive investigation of endogenous antioxidant systems, particularly the glutathione peroxidase (GPx)/total antioxidant status (TAS) and related peroxidases, could uncover synergistic mechanisms. Developing organelle-specific delivery platforms may further optimize therapeutic efficacy in oxidative retinal injury models. Second, while the SI-induced acute model has provided valuable mechanistic insights, its limitations in modeling the chronic, multifactorial nature of human dry AMD should be acknowledged. Complementary model systems that better recapitulate disease progression will be crucial for translating these antioxidant strategies into clinically viable therapies.”

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The study reports that dual-enzyme (CAT/SOD) delivery via nanocages can reduce oxidative injury in a sodium iodate-induced acute retinal injury model. However, due to fundamental flaws in experimental design, model choice, and data interpretation, these results cannot be considered reliable or generalizable to human GA/AMD. The study overinterprets acute toxin-induced injury as a model for GA/AMD, and its findings do not provide a clear advance over established antioxidant delivery studies.
The conclusions regarding therapeutic potential for dry AMD are unsupported. Key claims rely on misapplied animal and cellular models, schematic figures that may mislead readers, and incomplete or misinterpreted imaging and functional data. While the authors corrected several points to accommodate the concerns, overall credibility is diminished by rewriting and over-simplifications in response to prior criticisms. Multiple conceptual, methodological, and interpretive flaws remain, including inappropriate use of the SI model to mimic GA, overemphasis on vascular outcomes, missing statistical analyses in main figures, and schematics that do not clearly depict experimental or anatomical reality.
Methodological concerns include use of irrelevant in vitro cell types, incomplete descriptions of imaging and electrophysiology protocols, and misrepresentation of animal pathology. Although some methodological details have been clarified, critical information remains inconsistent or inaccurate, particularly regarding relevant cell types, imaging quantification, and schematic representation of enzyme delivery. Consequently, reproducibility is not ensured, and the manuscript does not meet field standards.
The authors’ responses and revisions do not adequately address key conceptual, methodological, and technical concerns raised in prior rounds. Overall, the manuscript's conclusions regarding therapeutic efficacy for dry AMD remain unsupported.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
This manuscript offers compelling evidence that a zwitterionic nanocage-based peroxidase eye drop therapy could be a game-changer for treating oxidative stress-related retinal diseases. These diseases may include geographic atrophy (GA) and dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). The work addresses a pressing gap in ophthalmology—therapeutic options for dry AMD remain scarce. By pairing an innovative delivery platform with a deeper understanding of oxidative injury, this study could really move the needle in the field.
The authors thoughtfully build on earlier antioxidant strategies. These include inorganic nanozymes such as Pt-, RhZ-, and CeO₂-based systems, which have struggled with poor biocompatibility and questionable efficacy. The zwitterionic nanocage platform sidesteps many of these issues. It boosts molecular stability, tissue permeability, and catalytic activity, making it a more practical therapeutic option. The non-invasive eye drop formulation improves patient compliance and accessibility, especially for people in the early stages of disease who hesitate to pursue more invasive treatments. After incorporating and addressing the reviewers' comments, the work is substantially more coherent.
That said, there are some limitations worth addressing to strengthen the translational relevance of these findings. The authors lean heavily on the sodium iodate (NaIO₃) model. While this model is widely used and practical for inducing RPE degeneration, it doesn’t fully mirror human AMD. NaIO₃ causes acute, chemically driven oxidative injury, leading to rapid RPE death. This occurs through apoptosis, necroptosis, and ferroptosis. Human AMD, on the other hand, unfolds slowly and involves a complex mix of lipid and protein buildup, chronic inflammation, complement dysregulation, and genetic factors. Also, NaIO₃ results are highly dose-dependent and can vary significantly from animal to animal. So the model captures only one piece of the AMD puzzle and might make the therapy appear more robust than it would be in chronic, real-world disease. These limitations don’t undermine the study, but they do suggest the authors should be cautious about claims of disease modification. The response to the review does not fully cover this.
The modified experimental design, data analysis, and interpretation are rigorous and well supported by the evidence presented. The reported therapeutic efficacy, tissue penetration, and non-invasive nature of the nanocage eye drops are convincingly demonstrated. However, the study evaluates treatment effects over only two weeks. This interval is insufficient to model the long-term progression of GA or dry AMD. Extending the treatment and follow-up durations would substantially strengthen the conclusions and better reflect clinical conditions. To clarify mechanisms, further studies should analyze the roles of endogenous antioxidant pathways and organelle-specific effects, and examine how the nanocage formulation interfaces with oxidative and inflammatory cascades.
For transparency and reproducibility, the authors should include details of how they calculated sample sizes and explain their rationale for selecting specific statistical methods. Clearly justifying these decisions and ensuring adequate statistical power and rigor will help build confidence in the reported therapeutic effects.
Overall, this manuscript presents a really innovative therapeutic strategy with strong potential to shape AMD research and clinical practice. While there’s more work to be done, especially in chronic disease models, mechanistic validation, and longer-term studies, the approach is scientifically sound. The findings are compelling. With revisions that address the concerns I’ve outlined, this study would be a valuable addition to Nature Communications and the broader vision science community.

Reply: We are deeply appreciative of the reviewer’s thoughtful and constructive evaluation, as well as the encouraging recognition of our work’s potential impact. The insightful suggestions have been invaluable in strengthening the translational relevance and mechanistic depth of our study. Below, we provide a point-by-point response to the specific concerns raised, detailing the revisions and additional experiments we have conducted.
1. Model terminology, limitations, and claims of disease modification.
We fully agree with the reviewer that the sodium iodate (NaIO₃) model represents an acute chemical injury and does not fully recapitulate the slow, multifactorial pathogenesis of human geographic atrophy (GA) or dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). In the revised manuscript, we have consistently replaced “GA mouse model” with “NaIO₃-induced acute retinal injury model (ARI)” in the text, titles, and figures. More importantly, we have added a dedicated subsection in the Discussion as following, where we explicitly acknowledge that this model primarily mirrors the oxidative stress component of retinal degeneration, and avoided over-interpreting its direct equivalence to chronic human disease. We clarify that our study is a mechanistic proof-of-concept designed to validate whether targeted enzyme delivery can ameliorate oxidative stress in the retina—but a key driver in GA pathogenesis.
“In the acute retinal injury model designed to recapitulate the reactive oxygen species (ROS)-induced degeneration pathology of GA, we consistently observed that restoration of the enzymatic cascade represents a promising therapeutic strategy for this condition.”
“Collectively, our findings demonstrate that the zwitterionic nanocage platform enables effective topical delivery of antioxidant enzymes to the retina, presenting a promising therapeutic strategy for mitigating oxidative stress-related retinal damage. While the SI-induced acute oxidative injury model serves as a valuable tool for investigating oxidative stress, a key driver of RPE and photoreceptor degeneration, it represents a simplified, accelerated system that lacks the chronic, multifactorial complexity of human dry AMD. Future studies will need to validate this proof-of-concept in more physiologically relevant chronic models that better mimic the slow human disease progression. Nonetheless, by addressing the critical challenge of ocular drug delivery, our platform provides a versatile and patient-friendly foundation for developing disease-modifying therapies for dry AMD.”
2. Treatment duration and long-term therapeutic evaluation
We really appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment regarding the limited observation window for modeling chronic disease progression. In response, we would like to highlight that during the preliminary phase of this study, we conducted an exploratory extended-duration experiment in which mice were treated with Z(CAT&SOD) for one month following NaIO₃-induced injury (Figure R1). Intriguingly, while this longer-term assessment confirmed sustained preservation of retinal structure and function compared to controls, the therapeutic benefits plateaued after the initial two-week period. We ultimately selected the two-week endpoint for the main study based on following reasons: (i) this duration aligns with the acute progression of NaIO₃-induced retinal injury, (ii) the two-week data robustly demonstrates the fundamental efficacy of our delivery platform, and (iii) this approach adheres to the 3R principles (Replacement, Reduction, Refinement) by minimizing animal use while maintaining scientific validity.
Figure R1. Representative fundus images and OCT images of mice after different treatments at (a) two weeks and (c) one month. Statistical analysis of retinal thickness of mice in different groups at (b) two weeks and (d) one month (n=6). Data were represented as means ± SD. P values in (c, d, e and g) were calculated by using one-way ANOVA.
3. Elucidation of endogenous antioxidant pathways and organelle-specific effects
In response to the reviewer’s valuable suggestion regarding mechanistic insights, we examined the effect of the zwitterionic nanocage’s internalization into cells on the mitochondria. We evaluated the subcellular localization of Z(CAT) labeled with Cy5.5 in RPE cells using confocal microscopy with a mitochondrial tracker (Figure R2). The imaging showed minimal mitochondrial accumulation of the nanocage, indicating that its therapeutic mechanism does not rely on direct organelle targeting. Instead, the nanocage predominantly localized to the cytosol and peri-mitochondrial space, a critical region for ROS diffusion and redox signaling. This spatial distribution is particularly beneficial for catalase activity, as ROS generated in mitochondria readily into the cytosol, where excessive accumulation amplifies oxidative stress and inflammatory signaling. By scavenging cytosolic ROS, our strategy indirectly mitigates oxidantive damage while preserving mitochondrial homeostasis.
To further characterize the therapeutic mechanism of Z(CAT&SOD), we conducted systematic analyses of endogenous antioxidant responses and mitochondrial protection in oxidatively stressed RPE cells. Quantitative PCR revealed that SI-induced oxidative stress triggered a robust activation of the Nrf2/ARE pathway, as evidenced by the significant upregulation of Nrf2 and its downstream targests (HMOX-1, NQO1, GCLC, and GPX1). Notably, this oxidative stress response was effectively attenuated by both free enzymes and Z(CAT&SOD), with the zwitterion-protected formulation exhibiting superior efficacy (Figure R3a). We next evaluated mitochondrial protection by measuring membrane potential and ROS generation. While confocal imaging confirmed minimal mitochondrial accumulation of Z(CAT&SOD), functional assays revealed its potent ability to preserve mitochondrial membrane integrity and attenuate secondary ROS production (Figure R3b). These findings demonstrate the therapeutic advantage of Z(CAT&SOD) in preventing mitochondrial oxidative damage by effectively scavenging cytosolic ROS without requiring direct organelle targeting..
We have integrated these findings into the Results and Discussion, expanding our mechanistic narrative from one of mere “replacement” to “activation and synergy” with endogenous systems.
“To investigate potential organelle-specific effects, we incubated RPE19 cells with Cy5.5 labeled Z(CAT) for 6 hours and performed mitochondrial co-localization analysis using a mitochondrial tracker. Confocal imaging revealed minimal mitochondrial accumulation of the nanocages (Supplementary Fig. 8), indicating that their therapeutic mechanism does not rely on direct mitochondrial targeting. Instead, the nanocage predominantly localized to the cytosol and peri-mitochondrial space, a critical region for ROS diffusion and redox signaling. This spatial distribution is particularly advantageous for catalase activity, as it positions the therapeutic agent near the sites of ROS generation while allowing for effective diffusion throughout the cytosol. To further characterize the cellular response to treatment, we analyzed the activation of endogenous antioxidant pathways in oxidatively stressed RPE cells after Z(CAT&SOD) treatment using qPCR. RPE cells were first treated with 200 μg/mL SI for 6 hours to induce oxidative stress, followed by treatment with free CAT&SOD or Z(CAT&SOD) for additional 6 hours. The qPCR analysis revealed that Z(CAT&SOD) treatment significantly downregulated the Nrf2 pathway and its downstream targets (e.g. GPX1, NQO1, GCLC, HMOX-1) (Supplementary Fig. 9a). This oxidative stress induction was effectively attenuated by both free CAT/SOD and the zwitterion-protected formulation, with the latter exhibiting superior protective efficacy, likely due to enhanced enzyme stability and improved cellular delivery. To further evaluate mitochondrial protection, we analyzed mitochondria integrity in stressed RPE cells after Z(CAT&SOD) treatment (Supplementary Fig. 9b). Although the nanocage does not directly localize to mitochondria, its cytosolic ROS-scavenging activity effectively preserved mitochondrial membrane potential and reduced secondary mitochondrial ROS production. These findings highlight the significant organelle-protective mechanism, reinforcing the therapeutic potential of our platform.”
“In summary, this study demonstrated that the pathogenesis of ARI is characterized by excessive retinal ROS production and reduced peroxidase activity. Our therapeutic intervention with CAT and SOD exhibits multi-model protection effects by effectively mitigating oxidative stress and inflammation responses while reducing cellular apoptosis and preserving mitochondrial protection. These findings establish a comprehensive antioxidant therapeutic approach for ARI management.”
Figure R2. Tracing of zwitterionic nanocage and mitochondria within RPE cells.
Figure R3. (a) Relative GPX1, GCLC, Nrf, NQO1 and HMOX-1 mRNA abundance (2-ΔΔCt) in RPE cells with different treatments. (b) Mitochondrial damage changes in RPE cells with different treatments.
4. Statistical transparency and reproducibility
In response to the reviewer’s request, we have expanded the Methods section to provide a complete description of our statistical analysis framework. This include the rationale for sample size determination and the selection of specific statistical tests (including one-way, two-way and t-test). To ensure full compliance with journal policy and maximal transparency, we have prepared a comprehensive Source Data file containing all individual quantitative measurements underlying the graphical representations. This dataset is accompanied by detailed annotations specifying the exact statistical test applied to each comparison.
Once again, we extend our sincere gratitude to Reviewer #4 for the exceptionally constructive and forward-looking critique, which has substantially elevated the quality of our manuscript. We believe the revised version, with its clarified scope, deeper mechanistic insight, and enhanced transparency, now offers a compelling and robust case for the therapeutic potential of our zwitterionic nanocage platform.

Responses to reviewer’s comments
We sincerely thank the reviewers for the valuable comments and suggestions. Below we have provided
point-to-point responses to the comments and have revised the manuscript accordingly.
Reviewer #1:
The manuscript presents an approach to mitigate oxidative stress-induced retinal degeneration
through co-encapsulation of catalase (CAT) and superoxide dismutase (SOD) in polymeric nanocages.
While antioxidant supplementation in retinal disease is a well-explored area, the co-delivery of these
these
two enzymes within a single carrier represents a technically interesting strategy that could have
therapeutic potential. However, several major concerns must be addressed before the manuscript can
be considered for publication.
1. First, the nanocages are composed of acrylamide and bisacrylamide-based polymers, materials
known to have neurotoxic properties. The manuscript does not sufficiently address the safety or
biocompatibility of these polymers for intraocular use, which is essential for translational relevance.
Additionally, although the title refers to an eye drop-based therapy, the data presented are limited to
intravitreal delivery; this discrepancy is misleading and should be clarified.
Reply: Thanks so much for the reviewer’s suggestion. We fully agree that the safety profile of any
intraocular or topical ophthalmic formulation is of utmost importance for its translational potential.
While acrylamide and bisacrylamide monomers have been associated with neurotoxicity in their
unpolymerized forms, it is important to emphasize that the polymerized forms used in our nanocage
system are chemically stable macromolecules that are not expected to exert systemic toxicity under
normal physiological conditions. To directly address this concern, we conducted a comprehensive 4-
week ocular and systemic safety evaluation of both empty zwitterionic nanocages and Z(CAT&SOD)
nanocages following topical ocular administration in healthy mice. The results showed that there were
no significant abnormalities observed in any of the tested parameters. Both empty and enzyme-loaded
nanocages were well-tolerated, with no signs of ocular irritation, no increase in IOP, no corneal or
retinal damage, and no systemic toxicity (Figure R1). These findings were consistent with previous
reports demonstrating that zwitterionic polymers exhibit excellent biocompatibility, low
immunogenicity, and minimal protein adsorption, making them suitable for biomedical applications,
including ocular drug delivery.
Furthermore, we sincerely apologize for any confusion caused by our title regarding the administration
method in this study. In this manuscript, intravitreal injection was used as a proof-of-concept to
rigorously evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of enzyme-loaded nanocages for dry AMD. Considering
the clinical preference for non-invasive therapies, we finally developed and optimized a topical eye
drop formulation using the same zwitterionic nanocage platform. Notably, this formulation
demonstrated promising therapeutic efficacy in treating oxidative stress-induced dry macular
degeneration in mice.
“Given the high sensitivity of ocular tissues, we conducted a thorough biocompatibility assessment of
Z(CAT&SOD) to ensure its safety for long-term use. A battery of ophthalmic evaluations including
slit-lamp microscope, optical coherence tomography (OCT), electroretinogram (ERG) and intraocular
pressure (IOP), were performed on mice four weeks after treatment with Z-polymer and Z(CAT&SOD)
eyedrops. As illustrated in Figure S14a and S14b, the corneas of treated mice remained clear and intact,
with no observable differences compared to healthy controls. Moreover, prolonged administration of
Z-polymer and Z(CAT&SOD) did not obviously alter tear secretion (Figure S14c). Corneal OCT
imaging confirmed that neither formation affected corneal thickness (Figure S14d and S14e), while
fundus imaging and retina thickness measurements revealed no structural abnormalities (Figure S14f
to S14i). In addition, IOP values remained stable after long-term treatment, indicating that the
Z(CAT&SOD) eyedrop dose not induce ocular hypertension or increase the risk of glaucoma (Figure
S14j). To assess systemic toxicity, we performed histological analysis of major organs (heart, liver,
spleen, lung, kidney and eye) via H&E staining. Tissues form Z-polymer and Z(CAT&SOD)-treated
mice exhibited nearly no pathological changes compared to healthy mice (Figure S14k). Additionally,
hematological analysis of blood samples confirmed that all parameters remained in the normal range,
indicating negligible systemic toxicity even after prolonged subconjunctival retention (Figure S14l).
Therefore, these findings demonstrate that both Z-polymer and Z(CAT&SOD) exhibit excellent
biocompatibility after long-term administration.”

contains multiple errors in ocular definitions and physiological interpretations, which diminish
confidence in the scientific rigor. For example, retinal ganglion cells are not the primary cells affected
in geographic atrophy (GA); the a-wave of the ERG is primarily associated with photoreceptor
(particularly rod) activity, not cones; and the b-wave is typically driven by bipolar cells rather than
directly by rods. Furthermore, evaluating choroidal neovascularization (CNV) as an outcome measure

inaccuracies suggest a need for more careful literature review and refinement of disease-

5) The study employs a sodium iodate-induced model of dry macular degeneration, which

Reply: Thanks so much for the reviewer’s comment. Sodium iodate (NaIO₃) serves as a well-
characterized oxidative stress inducer that selectively targets the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE),
initiating a degenerative cascade that faithfully recapitulates the cardinal features of human geographic
atrophy (GA)1. The mechanistic underpinnings of this model involve three interrelated pathological
proceess: 1) NaIO₃-mediated ROS overproduction induces RPE mitochondrial dysfunction, membrane
depolarization, and subsequent necroptotic cell death6; 2) secondary photoreceptor degeneration
occurs through disrupted retinoid cycling and loss of metabolic support, manifesting as outer nuclear
layer (ONL) thinning and diminished a-wave amplitudes on ERG; and 3) sustained neuroinflammation
develops via microglial activation, Muller cell gliosis, and macrophage infiltration, accompanied by
elevated inflammatory mediators (IL-1β, CCL2, IL-33, and TGF-β)7,8. This mark of RPE dysfunction,
photoreceptor loss, and chronic inflammation mirrors both the structural and dysfunction,
photoreceptor loss, and chronic inflammation indicated both the structural and functional deficits
observed in GA patient9. The NaIO₃ model thus provides a robust preclinical platform that captures
the complex pathophysiology of dry AMD, particularly for evaluating antioxidant therapies targeting
oxidative stress-mediated degeneration. We have added the related discussion in the revised
manuscript as following:
“The SI-induced GA model faithfully recapitulated key clinical manifestations of human GA,
including subretinal deposits and retinal atrophy. Through mechanistic studies, we identified two
critical pathologies features: oxidative stress-medicated apoptosis in both RPE and photoreceptor cells
and severe deficiency of endogenous antioxidant defenses (CAT/SOD). Notably, our therapeutic
experiments established that photoreceptor survival could be improved through antioxidant
supplementation during the critical window of oxidative stress dominance.”

Reviewer #3:
This study presents an interesting and potentially translationable strategy for the treatment of
geographic atrophy by constructing a zwitterionic nanocage-based delivery system that enables non-
invasive co-delivery of catalase (CAT) and superoxide dismutase (SOD) to the retina. The work
demonstrates strong innovation, solid in vivo data, and a relatively in-depth mechanistic exploration.
However, several scientific and mechanistic issues still need to be clarified or reinforced, and some
aspects of data presentation require revision. I recommend accept this manuscript after addressing
the following specific comments:
1) The manuscript emphasizes the synergistic effect of CAT and SOD as an enzymatic cascade.
However, there is no quantitative analysis confirming whether the combined use is superior to
individual enzymes in terms of ROS scavenging efficiency (e.g., rate of radical elimination, half-life of
ROS). It is recommended to include in vitro kinetic assays to validate whether this is a true cascade
reaction or simply an additive effect.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for this critical point. While we acknowledge that direct kinetic data
would further strengthen our mechanistic interpretation, our results demonstrate that the SOD-CAT
cascade operates through functional complementarity. Specifically, CAT converts the toxic byproduct
of SOD activity (H₂O₂) into harmless H₂O and O₂, thereby protecting SOD from oxidative inactivation
and ensuring sustained antioxidant capacity. This cooperative mechanism prevents •OH generation via
Fenton reaction, achieving complete ROS detoxification. To validate this synergy, we evaluated the
ROS-scavenging capacity of Z(CAT), Z(SOD), and Z(CAT&SOD) nanocages. As shown in Figure
R10, both modified enzymes retained their catalytic efficiency: SOD effectively eliminated superoxide
anions, while CAT degraded H₂O₂. Notably, the combined system (Z(CAT&SOD)) exhibited enhanced
radical scavenging, demonstrating cooperative action for optimal free radical elimination.

5）The sodium iodate-induced model used in this study mimics acute oxidative damage and may
primarily represent late-stage GA. Please discuss the limitations of this model in simulating the
chronic progression of GA and whether the proposed therapeutic strategy could be effective in early-
stage disease (e.g., before lipofuscin accumulation).
Reply: Thanks for pointing out this. While the sodium iodate model rapidly induces RPE and
photoreceptor degeneration that mimics late-stage geographic atrophy, its acute oxidative insult fails
to recapitulate the chronic, low-grade oxidative stress underlying human disease progression,
particularly the gradual lipofuscin accumulation characteristic of early pathogenesis9. We therefore
recognize this as a key limitation: while our data demonstrate therapeutic efficacy under acute,
advanced-like conditions, they do not address intervention efficacy during the critical pre-lipofuscin.
Notably, the CAT/SOD cascade specifically targets the ROS implicates in lipofuscinogenesis10,11. This
suggests that prophylactic administration of Z(CAT&SOD) during early-stage dry AMD could
effectively mitigate disease progression by neutralizing free radical before irreversible damage occurs.

GA patients, including subretinal deposits and retinal atrophy. Mechanistic investigations revealed that
RPE and photoreceptor cell apoptosis was closely associated with the microenvironment characterized
by high oxidative stress and diminished peroxidase activity, particularly reduced levels of CAT and
SOD. As a proof-of-concept, our findings suggest that timely antioxidant supplementation may
preserve residual photoreceptors when oxidative damage as the primary driver of degeneration.”

2. FFA detects vascular abnormalities; in SI-treated mice, increased FFA reflects RPE barrier

Reply: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment, which allows us to better clarify a
critical aspect of our experimental model. We fully agree that in typical human geographic atrophy
(GA), increased FFA signal is primarily attributed to RPE barrier disruption rather than
neovascularization. However, it’s important to note that the sodium iodate (SI)-induced model in our
study, while effectively mimicking oxidative stress-driven photoreceptor/RPE degeneration
characteristic GA, often elicits a more extensive secondary inflammatory response involving retinal
vasculature. The vascular abnormalities we observed via FFA (has been changed as “vascular
inflammation” or “secondary vascular abnormalities” in the revised main text) do not represent
neovascularization, but rather reflect inflammation-associated vascular leakage specific in this model.
The observed fluorescence enhancement indeed stems from blood-retinal barrier disruption,
encompassing both RPE and endothelial cell damage under inflammatory conditions. Here, FFA
serves as a valuable in vivo method to evaluate the extent of secondary vascular inflammation and
overall blood-retinal barrier integrity, both important indicators of retinal health in our model. We
have moved this data to Supporting Information to avoid overstating its role in the core narrative of
GA-like atrophy, while still presenting it as a supporting metric of disease severity and treatment
efficacy against the multifaceted insult induced by SI.
We have carefully revised the manuscript to clarify that the FFA findings reflect model-specific
